reading.body:
Government AI activity is now a matter of public record: federal agencies disclose what they run, GAO audits those inventories, and 2,425 state AI bills are tracked to their source.

The pattern is layered oversight. GAO reviews federal AI inventories and management, state legislation is tracked bill by bill, and international indexes from Oxford Insights, OECD.AI, and Stanford HAI compare national readiness, strategies, and policy execution. This makes government AI adoption measurable and auditable, which shapes where and how public-sector systems can operate.

What this record does not show is the physical layer. The Oxford Insights index scores infrastructure as one dimension, but no scores or infrastructure findings appear here. The data covers governance, law, and policy, not the compute, buildings, or power behind the systems being governed.

summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured picture of AI in government comes from the U.S. GAO's review of federal agencies. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, defined as specific challenges or opportunities AI may solve, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of those use cases were still in the planning phase rather than in production, and in about 200 instances agencies reported they were currently using AI. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Reported applications included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers.

The same GAO work shows the data quality behind those numbers is uneven. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with some inventories missing required elements such as the AI life cycle stage or whether a use case was releasable. Two inventories included AI uses that agencies later determined were not AI. GAO also found that no government-wide guidance exists on how agencies should acquire and use AI, and that until all requirements are met agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits. On implementation, Commerce and the General Services Administration fully implemented selected requirements, with Commerce creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA establishing an AI Center of Excellence, while OMB had not yet developed acquisition and use guidance and OPM had not established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt.

The most visible public-facing deployment is America.gov, launched September 29, 2026 by the General Services Administration and the National Design Studio under an executive order, per the White House fact sheet. It is described as a single digital point of entry where an individual can sign in, communicate in plain language, receive accurate answers, and, where authorized and technically available, complete government transactions without navigating multiple agency websites. The fact sheet states it runs on Google Gemini and xAI Grok and draws on about 29,000 government websites, with Phase 1 finding information and Phase 2, planned for 2027 with Login.gov, handling applications and renewals such as passport renewal and Medicare enrollment. Covered services are defined as public-facing federal services serving more than 100,000 users in a 12-month period that can be accessed or applied for online, with IRS tax filing and national-security-sensitive services at the Department of War and the Intelligence Community excluded. The site's own tracking notes America.gov offers no public API and its terms bar automated agents, so it is treated as a deployment rather than a source.

On the policy and oversight side, the sources describe infrastructure rather than outcomes. Stanford HAI's AI Index describes its mission as providing unbiased, rigorously vetted, and globally sourced data for policymakers and others, and states that this year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it, with governance, evaluation, and understanding frameworks falling behind while data transparency declines. OECD.AI, the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, says it helps countries shape trustworthy AI with the OECD AI Principles and gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI, and a policy blog, and notes that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand. Oxford Insights describes its work helping governments increase the impact of public services by empowering teams and harnessing technology. None of these three sources reports a government adoption rate or ROI figure in the material provided.

The regulatory posture is documented most concretely on this site's own AI laws tracking. It counts 6,074 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan, and a comparison of 113 measures across 28 states reviewed on September 18, 2026, finding that no two states wrote the same law. Only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149; every other measure names one setting such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom, or a state agency. Where stakes are personal, the recurring rule is that AI may assist but may not be the only decider: insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone under AL SB63 and IA HF2635, AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician under IL HB1806, TN HB1470, and CA AB489, it cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation under IL HB1859 and IL SB2909, and New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions under NY S07599. No state in the set created a new agency to enforce AI law; attorneys general enforce the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states declare a violation an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few practical conclusions and little more. The federal record shows adoption is real but mostly planned rather than in production, and that inventories of what is actually running are frequently incomplete, so internal record-keeping is a genuine gap to close. The recurring statutory pattern across states is disclosure that a person is dealing with AI, a qualified human in any decision about health, employment, benefits, or education, a crisis protocol and age awareness for conversational products, and retained records, with the attorney general as the enforcer most likely to be encountered. The sources here do not report government-specific ROI figures, cost savings, or error rates, so any claim about returns from public-sector AI deployment would go beyond what this material shows.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI describes itself as a policy observatory that helps countries shape trustworthy AI in line with the OECD AI Principles, and says it offers access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, live data about AI and a blog on AI policy. It invites organisations developing advanced AI systems to take part by submitting a report, saying that sharing information would help make risk mitigation measures more transparent and comparable. The observatory states that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI combined under the GPAI brand into one integrated partnership. Its stated purpose is to help AI actors build and use systems that respect human rights and are fair, transparent, explainable, robust, secure and safe.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index at Stanford HAI describes its mission as supplying unbiased, globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public, tracking and visualising data on the field. This year's edition, the page says, shows a widening gap between what AI can do and our readiness to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while governance and evaluation frameworks lag. The page states that previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It describes the programme as an independent Stanford HAI initiative led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, and notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez on regulatory frameworks.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-laws/.brief: The page reports that 6,074 artificial intelligence bills are tracked across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database and linked to each bill's official page. It says a comparison of enrolled text covered 113 measures across 28 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026, and found no two states wrote the same law, though recurring choices appear. According to the page, only Colorado (CO SB189) and Texas (TX HB149) passed broad laws reaching consequential decisions across sectors, while other measures name a single setting such as a chatbot, political ad, insurance prior authorization, classroom or state agency. It states that no state in the set created a new agency to enforce AI law, with attorneys general enforcing the larger laws and several states treating violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
